narratives.name: Scrum Foundations Practice Narrative
narratives.description: The transformational journey of adopting Scrum for empirical product development.

narrativeContexts.context: Organizations face complex product development challenges where traditional predictive planning fails to manage uncertainty, requirements shift faster than plans can adapt, and teams lack the empowerment to make timely decisions based on emerging evidence.

Scrum introduces a radical departure from command-and-control project management by establishing an empirical framework where small, cross-functional teams self-manage their work within fixed-length Sprints, inspecting outcomes and adapting continuously based on what they learn from actual experience rather than speculative forecasts.

Teams navigate the transformation from predictive to empirical mindsets, confronting organizational resistance to self-management, learning to balance Sprint commitment with flexibility, establishing the discipline of a Definition of Done that never weakens under pressure, and building the trust required for Scrum Values to become behavioral reality rather than aspirational slogans.

Teams achieve sustainable, predictable delivery of valuable product Increments through internalized empiricism, where transparency, inspection, and adaptation are natural behaviors, stakeholders collaborate as active partners in product evolution, and continuous improvement compounds team effectiveness across every Sprint cycle.

narratives.name: Scrum Work Management Through Sprint-Based Delivery
narratives.description: How Scrum structures work through time-boxed Sprints with Sprint Goals providing coherence and focus.

narrativeContexts.context: Scrum structures work through time-boxed Sprints where teams commit to Sprint Goals that provide coherence and focus. The Sprint transforms work management from continuous flow into focused, inspectable increments of value delivery.

Within each Sprint, the team selects Product Backlog items during Sprint Planning, coordinates daily through the Daily Scrum, and produces at least one usable Increment. The Sprint Goal ensures the team delivers meaningful, coherent value rather than a collection of disconnected tasks.
By constraining work within Sprint boundaries and enforcing the Definition of Done, Scrum ensures completed work is genuinely done and provides a reliable foundation for empirical progress tracking.

narratives.name: The Self-Managing Scrum Team
narratives.description: How the Scrum Team operates as a self-managing, cross-functional unit with three accountabilities.

narrativeContexts.context: The Scrum Team is a self-managing, cross-functional unit of ten or fewer people with no sub-teams or hierarchies. The three accountabilities of Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers create a balanced structure for iterative value delivery.

Self-management means the team internally decides who does what, when, and how without external prescription. The five Scrum Values of Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect, and Courage guide team interactions and build the trust necessary for empirical process control to succeed.
A well-functioning Scrum Team continuously improves its effectiveness through Sprint Retrospectives, embedding improvement actions into subsequent Sprint Backlogs to compound gains over time.

narratives.name: Empirical Process Control as Way Of Working
narratives.description: How Scrum establishes empiricism and lean thinking as the foundation for the team's way of working.

narrativeContexts.context: Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking, replacing predictive planning with transparency, inspection, and adaptation. The framework prescribes five events, three artifacts, and three commitments as the minimum structure for empirical process control.

Each Scrum event creates a formal opportunity to inspect and adapt Scrum artifacts, while the artifacts themselves provide the transparency necessary for informed decisions. The five Scrum Values of Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect, and Courage create the environment in which empirical practices can succeed and trust can develop.

Continuous improvement is embedded in Scrum through the Sprint Retrospective, where the team identifies actionable improvements and plans them into subsequent Sprints, ensuring the way of working evolves with each iteration.

narratives.name: The Sprint as Heartbeat of Scrum
narratives.description: How the Sprint creates consistency and predictability through fixed-length time-boxed iterations.

narrativeContexts.context: The Sprint is the heartbeat of Scrum, a fixed-length event of one month or less where ideas are turned into value, creating consistency and predictability for the team and its stakeholders. Each Sprint serves as a short project with bounded scope, cost, and duration, limiting risk while generating learning cycles.

Sprints operate as containers for all other Scrum events, establishing an unbroken cadence of delivery with no gaps between iterations. Four invariants are maintained during each Sprint: the Sprint Goal remains protected, quality never decreases, the Product Backlog is refined as needed, and scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner. Shorter Sprints generate more learning cycles and limit risk, while longer Sprints may cause complexity to rise. The Sprint time-box gives teams the ability to forecast and improve through empirical evidence of capacity and trajectory.

Sprint optimization is a progressive journey from establishing basic cadence through maintaining invariants to achieving predictable delivery that stakeholders can rely upon for planning, ultimately enabling continuous value flow independent of the Sprint Review cycle.

narratives.name: The Definition of Done as Quality Commitment
narratives.description: How the Definition of Done functions as the commitment for the Increment artifact, ensuring transparency and quality.

narrativeContexts.context: The Definition of Done is the commitment for the Increment artifact, elevated in the 2020 Scrum Guide alongside the Product Goal and Sprint Goal as one of three artifact commitments. It creates transparency by providing a shared understanding of what work was completed as part of the Increment.

The Definition of Done functions as an absolute binary quality gate -- there is no concept of partially done in Scrum. If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. This clarity prevents the accumulation of undone work, which Sutherland identifies as a primary driver of project failure. The Definition of Done should evolve through Sprint Retrospective insights, generally becoming more rigorous as the team's capability grows, but it should never be weakened to accommodate schedule pressure.

As a variant of Team Agreement, the Definition of Done follows the natural lifecycle from initial creation through formal adoption to continuous evolution, specialized for the critical concern of quality governance that ensures every Increment delivers genuine, usable value.

personas.name: Product Owner
personas.description: Maximizes product value through effective Product Backlog management and goal communication.

narratives.name: The Product Owner Accountability
narratives.description: How the Product Owner maximizes product value through backlog management and goal communication.

narrativeContexts.context: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team, serving as the single authority on what the product should become and in what order value should be delivered.

The Product Owner's specific accountabilities include developing and communicating the Product Goal, creating and communicating Product Backlog items, ordering Product Backlog items to maximize value, and ensuring the Product Backlog is transparent and understood. The Product Owner is one person, not a committee, ensuring clear decision-making authority that the organization must respect. During Sprint Planning, the Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value, and during the Sprint, collaborates with Developers on scope negotiation when work diverges from expectations.

The Product Owner represents the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog, and their decisions are visible in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog and through the inspectable Increment at Sprint Review.

personas.name: Scrum Master
personas.description: Establishes Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide and enables team effectiveness.

narratives.name: The Scrum Master as Servant-Leader
narratives.description: How the Scrum Master serves the team and organization through coaching, facilitation, and impediment removal.

narrativeContexts.context: The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide and for the Scrum Team's effectiveness, serving as a true leader who serves the team and the larger organization through coaching, facilitation, and impediment removal.

The Scrum Master's service spans three dimensions: serving the Scrum Team through coaching in self-management and cross-functionality; serving the Product Owner through techniques for effective backlog management and stakeholder collaboration; and serving the organization through leading Scrum adoption, removing barriers between stakeholders and teams, and helping employees understand empirical approaches. The Scrum Master causes the removal of impediments, ensures events are positive and productive, and coaches team members to develop their Scrum practice within the framework.
The servant-leadership model means the Scrum Master leads by enabling rather than directing, shaping both the team's internal dynamics and the organizational environment in which the team operates.

personas.name: Developer
personas.description: Creates any aspect of a usable Increment each Sprint as a development professional.

narratives.name: The Developer Accountability
narratives.description: How Developers create usable Increments through self-managed professional work.

narrativeContexts.context: Developers are the people in the Scrum Team committed to creating any aspect of a usable Increment each Sprint, where the term encompasses all specialists who contribute to creating the Increment regardless of their domain expertise.

Developers are accountable for creating the Sprint Backlog plan, instilling quality by adhering to the Definition of Done, adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal, and holding each other accountable as professionals. How work gets done is at the sole discretion of the Developers, and no one outside the team tells them how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value. During Sprint Planning, Developers select items and plan work; during Sprints, they participate in Daily Scrums; and they are responsible for sizing Product Backlog items during refinement.
The Developer accountability emphasizes professional responsibility where team members actively manage their work toward a shared objective rather than merely executing externally assigned tasks.

narratives.name: The Scrum Team as Fundamental Unit
narratives.description: How the Scrum Team operates as a cohesive, self-managing unit focused on delivering value each Sprint.

narrativeContexts.context: The Scrum Team is the fundamental unit of Scrum, a cohesive group of professionals with no sub-teams or hierarchies, focused on one objective at a time and accountable for creating a valuable Increment every Sprint.

The team is cross-functional, possessing all skills necessary to create value each Sprint without external dependencies, and self-managing, meaning members internally decide who does what, when, and how. The team size is typically 10 or fewer people, reflecting research that smaller teams communicate better and are more productive. The team is responsible for all product-related activities from stakeholder collaboration through verification, maintenance, and experimentation.

Working in Sprints at a sustainable pace improves focus and consistency, and if the team grows too large, it should reorganize into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams sharing the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner.

narratives.name: Sprint Planning Technique
narratives.description: How to conduct Sprint Planning addressing why, what, and how topics.

narrativeContexts.context: Sprint Planning initiates each Sprint by establishing why the Sprint is valuable, what can be done, and how the chosen work will get done, producing the Sprint Backlog as the output artifact.

The event addresses three topics in sequence. First, the Product Owner proposes how the product could increase value, and the team collaboratively crafts the Sprint Goal. Second, Developers select Product Backlog items for the Sprint through discussion with the Product Owner, decomposing and clarifying items as needed. Third, Developers plan the work necessary to create an Increment, typically breaking selected items into work units of one day or less. The Sprint Goal, selected items, and delivery plan together compose the Sprint Backlog.

Teams often skip the "why" topic and jump directly to item selection, producing Sprints without coherent goals. Overly detailed upfront planning contradicts empirical process control; the plan should be sufficient to start, not exhaustive.

narratives.name: Daily Scrum Technique
narratives.description: How to conduct the Daily Scrum as a Developer-owned planning event.

narrativeContexts.context: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for Developers held at the same time and place each working day to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary.

Developers choose whatever structure and techniques they want for the Daily Scrum as long as it focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produces an actionable plan for the next day of work. The event improves communication, identifies impediments, promotes quick decision-making, and consequently eliminates the need for other meetings. If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on Sprint Backlog items, they participate as Developers.

Treating the Daily Scrum as a status report to the Scrum Master rather than a planning event owned by Developers undermines self-management. Rigidly following the three-questions format when it no longer serves the team conflicts with empirical adaptation.

narratives.name: Sprint Review Technique
narratives.description: How to conduct the Sprint Review as a collaborative working session.

narrativeContexts.context: The Sprint Review is the second-to-last event of the Sprint where the Scrum Team presents work results to key stakeholders and together they discuss progress toward the Product Goal.

The Scrum Team presents the results of their work to stakeholders and discusses progress toward the Product Goal. The team and stakeholders collaboratively review what was accomplished and what has changed in the environment, then determine what to do next. The Product Backlog may be adjusted to meet new opportunities based on feedback received. The Sprint Review is a working session, not a presentation, and should generate rich dialogue about the product's direction.

Treating the Sprint Review as a demo or presentation rather than a collaborative working session limits the quality of stakeholder feedback. Excluding stakeholders or limiting attendance reduces the diversity of perspectives needed for effective Product Backlog adaptation.

narratives.name: Sprint Retrospective Technique
narratives.description: How to conduct the Sprint Retrospective for continuous improvement.

narrativeContexts.context: The Sprint Retrospective concludes each Sprint by providing the Scrum Team a structured opportunity to inspect itself and create a plan for improvements to enact during the next Sprint.

The Scrum Team inspects how the last Sprint went with regard to individuals, interactions, processes, tools, and their Definition of Done. The team identifies assumptions that led them astray and explores their origins, then discusses what went well, what problems were encountered, and how those problems were or were not solved. The most impactful improvements are identified and addressed as soon as possible, with the most helpful changes potentially added to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint.

Conducting retrospectives as complaint sessions without actionable outcomes produces cynicism and disengagement. Failing to follow through on identified improvements erodes trust in the retrospective process and the team's commitment to continuous improvement.

narratives.name: Product Backlog Refinement Technique
narratives.description: How to conduct ongoing Product Backlog refinement as a collaborative activity.

narrativeContexts.context: Product Backlog refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller more precise items, adding detail such as descriptions, order, and size as an ongoing activity.

Developers who will do the work are responsible for the sizing, while the Product Owner may influence sizing by helping Developers understand and select trade-offs. Refinement is performed as an ongoing activity throughout the Sprint, typically consuming no more than 10% of the Developers' capacity. Items are decomposed until they are transparent enough for selection during Sprint Planning, with sufficient detail for a single Sprint of work.

Treating refinement as a formal ceremony rather than an ongoing collaborative activity creates bottlenecks and reduces responsiveness. Over-refining items far into the future wastes effort on items whose requirements will likely change before selection.

narratives.description: How to establish and communicate a Product Goal as the long-term planning target.

narrativeContexts.context: The Product Goal describes a future state of the product that serves as a target for the Scrum Team to plan against, providing the long-term objective that gives meaning and direction to the Product Backlog.

The Product Owner develops and explicitly communicates the Product Goal, which is the commitment for the Product Backlog. A Scrum Team must fulfill or abandon one objective before taking on the next, ensuring focus and coherence. The Product Goal lives in the Product Backlog and the rest of the backlog emerges to define what will fulfill it, creating a hierarchy from strategic vision to actionable work items.

Setting Product Goals that are too vague to be measurable prevents the team from knowing when they have achieved their objective. Pursuing multiple Product Goals simultaneously dilutes focus and contradicts the Scrum principle of one objective at a time.

narratives.description: How to craft a Sprint Goal that provides focus, coherence, and flexibility.

narrativeContexts.context: The Sprint Goal is the single objective for the Sprint that provides focus and coherence, encouraging the Scrum Team to work together rather than on separate initiatives.

The Sprint Goal is crafted during Sprint Planning through collaboration among the entire Scrum Team. The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value and utility in the current Sprint, and the whole team then collaborates to define a Sprint Goal that communicates why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders. The Sprint Goal is the commitment for the Sprint Backlog, providing flexibility regarding the exact work needed to achieve it while maintaining a fixed objective.

Creating Sprint Goals that merely summarize selected items rather than expressing a coherent value proposition fails to provide meaningful direction. Sprint Goals that are too broad to be achievable within a single Sprint undermine the team's ability to demonstrate focused progress.

narratives.name: Definition of Done Establishment Technique
narratives.description: How to create a formal Definition of Done as a shared quality standard.

narrativeContexts.context: The Definition of Done is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product, creating transparency by providing a shared understanding of what work was completed as part of the Increment.

If the Definition of Done for an Increment is part of the standards of the organization, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum; if not, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product. The Developers are required to conform to the Definition of Done, and if multiple teams work together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done. The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born.

Defining "Done" too loosely allows technical debt to accumulate and produces Increments that require undone work before release. Failing to enforce the Definition of Done as a binary gate creates ambiguity about whether work is truly complete.

test.description: Verifies that Product Backlog items are ordered to maximize value delivery with transparent inspectable ordering.

Stakeholder feedback or market changes necessitate reordering

narratives.name: Product Backlog Ordering Technique
narratives.description: How to order the Product Backlog to maximize value delivery.

narrativeContexts.context: Product Backlog ordering is the Product Owner's continuous responsibility to arrange items so that the most valuable work is addressed first, ensuring the Scrum Team always works on the highest-impact items.

The Product Owner is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog, making decisions visible in the content and ordering of the backlog itself. Ordering considers multiple factors including business value, risk, dependencies, and learning needs, with the Product Owner balancing stakeholder needs against technical considerations. The ordered backlog serves as the single source of requirements for any changes to the product, with higher-ordered items being clearer and more detailed than lower-ordered ones.

Delegating ordering decisions to committees or stakeholder groups without clear Product Owner authority creates ordering paralysis. Ordering solely by stakeholder loudness rather than objective value analysis produces suboptimal value delivery sequences.

test.name: Increment Meets Definition of Done
test.description: Verifies that usable Increments are created that are additive to all prior Increments and work together coherently.
given: Developers are working on Product Backlog items during the Sprint
A Definition of Done is established and understood by all team members
when: Developers complete work on Product Backlog items and assess results against the Definition of Done
then: One or more usable Increments are created that are additive to all prior Increments and work together coherently

narratives.name: Increment Creation Technique
narratives.description: How to produce usable Increments meeting the Definition of Done.

narrativeContexts.context: An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal, where each Increment is additive to all prior Increments, thoroughly verified, and ensures that all Increments work together.

Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint, and the sum of the Increments is presented at the Sprint Review. Work cannot be considered part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done, which serves as a binary quality gate. An Increment may be delivered to stakeholders prior to the end of the Sprint, and the Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value. If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or presented at Sprint Review and returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

Treating the Increment as a partial or incomplete deliverable that requires additional work before it is usable contradicts the core Scrum principle of delivering done work. Allowing items that do not meet the Definition of Done to be counted as part of the Increment creates false progress signals and accumulates hidden technical debt.

narratives.name: Scrum Master Service Technique
narratives.description: How the Scrum Master serves the team, Product Owner, and organization.

narrativeContexts.context: The Scrum Master serves the Scrum Team by coaching members in self-management and cross-functionality, helping the team focus on creating high-value Increments, and causing the removal of impediments to the team's progress.

Service operates across three dimensions. For the Scrum Team, the Scrum Master coaches in self-management and cross-functionality, helps focus on high-value Increments meeting the Definition of Done, causes removal of impediments, and ensures all Scrum events take place and are positive, productive, and kept within the timebox. For the Product Owner, the Scrum Master helps find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management and facilitates stakeholder collaboration. For the organization, the Scrum Master leads, trains, and coaches the organization in its Scrum adoption and helps employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach.

Acting as a project manager who assigns tasks and tracks progress rather than a servant-leader who enables self-management undermines team autonomy. Focusing exclusively on internal team dynamics while neglecting organizational impediments limits the Scrum Master's effectiveness at removing systemic barriers.

narratives.name: Stakeholder Engagement Technique
narratives.description: How to ensure stakeholder participation and transparent collaboration.

narrativeContexts.context: Stakeholder engagement in Scrum ensures that those who can influence or are affected by the product actively participate in the inspect-and-adapt cycle, primarily through Sprint Review attendance and ongoing Product Backlog transparency.

The Scrum Master helps remove barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams, facilitating collaboration as requested or needed. The Product Owner represents the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog, ensuring their concerns are reflected in item content and ordering. The Sprint Review provides the primary forum for stakeholder engagement, where attendees collaborate with the Scrum Team on what to do next and the Product Backlog may be adjusted to meet newly identified opportunities.

Allowing stakeholders to bypass the Product Owner and directly assign work to Developers undermines the Product Backlog as the single source of requirements. Treating stakeholder engagement as a one-way reporting relationship rather than a collaborative inspect-and-adapt dialogue limits the value of feedback.

narratives.name: Sprint Backlog Adaptation Technique
narratives.description: How to adapt the Sprint Backlog while protecting the Sprint Goal.

narrativeContexts.context: Sprint Backlog adaptation is the continuous process of updating the Sprint plan as more is learned during the Sprint, ensuring the plan reflects current reality while the Sprint Goal remains the fixed commitment.

As Developers learn more during the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog is updated throughout to reflect current understanding. If work turns out to be different than expected, Developers collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog without affecting the Sprint Goal. The Sprint Backlog is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint, and it is updated at minimum at each Daily Scrum to reflect emerging understanding.

Treating the Sprint Backlog as frozen after Sprint Planning prevents the team from adapting to new information, contradicting the empirical nature of Scrum. Allowing scope changes to silently alter or compromise the Sprint Goal violates the Sprint Goal's role as the fixed commitment of the Sprint.

narratives.name: Sprint Cancellation Technique
narratives.description: How to handle Sprint cancellation when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.

narrativeContexts.context: A Sprint can be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, with only the Product Owner having the authority to cancel the Sprint, ensuring this significant decision has clear accountability.

Sprint cancellation occurs when organizational direction, market conditions, or technology changes render the Sprint Goal obsolete. Any completed and "Done" Product Backlog items are reviewed to determine if they constitute usable Increments; if so, the Product Owner typically accepts them. All incomplete items are re-evaluated and returned to the Product Backlog for future consideration. The team then regroups for a new Sprint Planning, consuming any already done work as part of the new Sprint's context.

Using Sprint cancellation as a routine mechanism to reset scope rather than as a rare response to truly obsolete goals undermines Sprint cadence and team stability. Failing to assess completed work for potential Increment value during cancellation wastes effort that may have produced usable functionality.

patterns.name: Sprint Lifecycle
patterns.description: The recurring cycle of Sprint events transforming ideas into valuable usable Increments through empirical planning, execution, inspection, and adaptation.

patternViews.name: Sprint Prerequisites
patternViews.description: All conditions necessary for Sprint execution are established, ensuring the team has the foundation to begin empirical product development.

narrativeContexts.context: Before the first Sprint can begin, the Scrum Team must be formed with all three accountabilities filled, the Product Backlog must contain ordered and refined items representing stakeholder needs, a Definition of Done must be agreed upon as the team's shared quality standard, and the foundational principles of empiricism and the Scrum Values must be understood as the basis for the team's way of working.

patternViews.name: Plan
patternViews.description: Sprint scope, goal, and delivery plan established collaboratively by the entire Scrum Team.

narrativeContexts.context: The Sprint begins with collaborative planning where the Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value, the whole Scrum Team defines a Sprint Goal communicating why the Sprint is valuable, Developers select items from the refined Product Backlog and decompose them into a delivery plan, and the Sprint Backlog emerges as the combination of the Sprint Goal, selected Product Backlog items, and the plan for delivering the resulting Increment.

patternViews.name: Do
patternViews.description: Developers execute the Sprint plan, creating usable Increments that meet the Definition of Done while maintaining Sprint invariants.

narrativeContexts.context: Developers execute the Sprint plan while maintaining the four Sprint invariants: the Sprint Goal is protected as the coherent objective, quality standards embodied in the Definition of Done never decrease, the Product Backlog is refined as needed to prepare future work, and scope is negotiated with the Product Owner as the team learns more about the work. Daily Scrums provide a 15-minute coordination cadence focused on progress toward the Sprint Goal, and usable Increments meeting the Definition of Done are created continuously throughout the Sprint.

patternViews.name: Check
patternViews.description: The Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect Sprint outcomes, collaborating on product direction and backlog adaptations.

narrativeContexts.context: The Scrum Team and key stakeholders convene in a working session to inspect the Sprint's Increment against the Product Goal, discuss progress and environmental changes affecting the product, and collaborate on what to do next. The Product Backlog is adjusted to address new opportunities and insights surfaced during the review, and stakeholder feedback directly influences future work ordering and the trajectory toward the Product Goal.

patternViews.name: Act
patternViews.description: The Scrum Team inspects its processes, interactions, and quality standards, planning concrete improvements for the next Sprint.

narrativeContexts.context: The Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint with the team inspecting individuals, interactions, processes, tools, and the Definition of Done against both what went well and what could be improved. The most impactful improvements are identified and committed to for the next Sprint, potentially added directly to the Sprint Backlog to ensure execution. The Scrum Master serves the team by facilitating this reflection, and the compounding effect of retrospective improvements drives the Sprint cadence toward predictable delivery rhythm.

patterns.name: Product Evolution Journey
patterns.description: Multi-Sprint progression from Product Goal definition through iterative delivery to goal achievement, tracing the team's arc from vision to validated value.

patternViews.name: Product Vision Prerequisites
patternViews.description: The organization identifies a product opportunity, assembles a Scrum Team, and establishes the initial conditions for empirical product development.

narrativeContexts.context: The organization has identified a product with a clear boundary and known stakeholders, a Product Owner is designated with accountability for maximizing the value the product delivers, a Scrum Team is assembled with all necessary cross-functional skills, and an initial understanding of the product's value proposition seeds the Product Backlog with early items that represent the first steps toward the Product Goal.

patternViews.name: Departure
patternViews.description: The Product Goal is established and initial Sprints begin, transitioning from conceptual vision to empirical product development.

narrativeContexts.context: The Product Owner communicates the Product Goal and begins ordering the Product Backlog to maximize value delivery, the team establishes its Definition of Done as a shared quality standard, Sprint cadence is selected, and the first Sprint Planning sessions translate vision into actionable Sprint Backlogs. The team is learning the rhythm of Scrum events while calibrating its capacity and refining its understanding of the work required to progress toward the Product Goal.

patternViews.name: Initiation
patternViews.description: The delivery cadence is established with stakeholder feedback flowing and the team developing cross-functional collaboration.

narrativeContexts.context: The team moves beyond initial learning into the challenge of sustaining empirical practices across Sprints, producing Increments that meet the Definition of Done, receiving and incorporating stakeholder feedback through Sprint Reviews, and beginning the compounding improvement cycle through Sprint Retrospectives. The four Sprint invariants are actively maintained, and the team discovers both the power and the difficulty of transparency, inspection, and adaptation as lived practice rather than theory.

patternViews.name: Transformation
patternViews.description: The team achieves self-management with empiricism internalized as a natural mindset rather than a prescribed process.

narrativeContexts.context: The transformation represents the shift from doing Scrum to being Scrum, where the Scrum Values of commitment, focus, openness, respect, and courage are embodied as behavioral reality rather than aspirational statements. The team operates as a cohesive professional unit making decisions based on empirical evidence, the Definition of Done has been strengthened through accumulated retrospective insights, stakeholders trust the team's delivery rhythm, and the Scrum Master's focus shifts from coaching fundamentals to removing organizational impediments and serving the broader organization's Scrum adoption.

patternViews.name: Return
patternViews.description: The Product Goal is achieved through accumulated Increments and learning, and the team's experience informs the next product evolution cycle.

narrativeContexts.context: The Product Goal is fulfilled through accumulated Increments validated by stakeholders across multiple Sprint Reviews, with the Product Owner evaluating fulfillment based on empirical evidence of value delivery. The Product Backlog has been optimized to reflect deep understanding of stakeholder needs and product capabilities, and the lessons from this product evolution cycle inform the next Product Goal definition, creating an organizational learning loop that elevates the team's capability for future product journeys.

patterns.name: Team Formation Journey
patterns.description: Progression from assembling a Scrum Team through establishing practices to performing cohesively, where the team internalizes empiricism and Scrum Values as behavioral reality.

patternViews.name: Organizational Commitment
patternViews.description: The organization decides to adopt Scrum, commits to empowering the team, and allocates resources for the three Scrum accountabilities.

narrativeContexts.context: The organization has decided to adopt Scrum for a product, committed to empowering the team to self-manage its work within the Scrum framework, and made appropriate people available to fill the Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developer accountabilities. The Scrum Master may begin serving the organization at this stage by leading, training, and coaching stakeholders and leaders in Scrum adoption and its implications for organizational structure.

patternViews.name: Assemble and Orient
patternViews.description: The Scrum Team is formed with all three accountabilities, foundational practices and agreements are established, and the first Sprint cadence is determined.

narrativeContexts.context: The Scrum Team comes together with one Product Owner, one Scrum Master, and Developers, totaling 10 or fewer people with all skills necessary to create value each Sprint. The Scrum Master coaches the team in Scrum theory, events, artifacts, and the empirical pillars, the team creates its initial Definition of Done as a shared formal quality standard, Sprint length is selected to maintain focus and reduce complexity, and working agreements are established that ground the Scrum Values in concrete behavioral expectations.

patternViews.name: Practice and Calibrate
patternViews.description: The team runs its first Sprints, experiencing the full Sprint lifecycle, calibrating capacity, and developing cross-functional collaboration through real experience.

narrativeContexts.context: The team runs its first Sprints experiencing the full cadence of Scrum events and calibrating its practices through empirical feedback. Sprint Planning teaches collaborative goal-setting and scope selection, Daily Scrums establish coordination rhythm focused on Sprint Goal progress, Sprint Reviews introduce stakeholder collaboration around usable Increments, and Sprint Retrospectives begin the compounding improvement cycle where the team inspects its own effectiveness and commits to concrete improvement actions.

patternViews.name: Mature and Optimize
patternViews.description: The team achieves sustained high performance with internalized empiricism, embodied Scrum Values, and evolved quality standards.

narrativeContexts.context: The team has transitioned from learning Scrum to being Scrum, with empirical process control as a natural decision-making mindset, the Scrum Values of commitment, focus, openness, respect, and courage embodied to the point where trust is present and the team self-corrects without external intervention. The Definition of Done has evolved through accumulated retrospective insights to reflect the team's growing capability and quality commitment, Sprint delivery has become predictable through disciplined practice, and the Scrum Master's focus has shifted from internal coaching to removing organizational impediments and facilitating the team's continued growth.
